title: Returning to Key Stage 3: A Curriculum Begins With an Entitlement
author: Sarah Findlater
summary: Findlater opens the first post in a seven-part series on reviewing her school's Key Stage 3 English curriculum and assessment, arguing that curriculum review should start with entitlement rather than assessment frameworks. She defines entitlement as the knowledge, disciplinary thinking, and growing independence every student should have the opportunity to develop, and argues it is the reference point that gives assessment judgments like "secure" real meaning. She distinguishes between a curriculum that merely has all its required documents in place and one that is genuinely coherent, where each part of learning visibly prepares students for what follows and teachers understand why content is sequenced as it is. Drawing on Mary Myatt's "From Coverage to Coherence," she contrasts two departments teaching identical units who nonetheless give students very different experiences depending on whether connections between units are made explicit. She closes with a set of questions departments should ask when reviewing curriculum and assessment, and frames the review as a cycle of continual refinement rather than a one-time fix, previewing the next post in the series on defining curriculum progression.
points: Argues curriculum review should begin with defining student entitlement rather than with assessment frameworks, because assessment judgments like "secure" are meaningless without a clear reference point for what students were entitled to learn.

Distinguishes an organized curriculum (all documents present) from a coherent one (each part of learning visibly builds toward and connects with what follows), citing Mary Myatt's "From Coverage to Coherence" as an influence.

Illustrates with a contrast between two departments teaching identical units and assessments who produce very different student experiences depending on whether connections between units are made explicit to students.

Frames entitlement as encompassing not just access to rich knowledge and texts but growing independence and disciplinary thinking, cautioning that familiarity should not set the boundary of what students encounter.

Provides a list of concrete review questions for departments and frames curriculum and assessment review as an annual cycle of continual refinement rather than a single fix, previewing progression as the next topic in the series.
quotes: I began this work by refining our approach to assessment, but it took me further back: to what every student should gain from studying the subject in the first place.
By entitlement, I mean the knowledge, disciplinary thinking and growing independence that every student should have the opportunity to develop.
Until teachers can answer that, ‘Secure’ risks becoming a polished reporting label rather than a meaningful judgement.
Entitlement provides the reference point. It connects assessment to the curriculum, rather than leaving it as a separate exercise in reporting.

A curriculum can appear organised because all the required documents exist. Coherence becomes visible when one part of the learning prepares students for what follows and when teachers understand why a text, concept or task belongs where it does.

Students in one may build knowledge they can draw on when they meet a new text, recognise connections and make more of the decisions for themselves. In other settings, the taught units may be worthwhile but remain separate in students’ minds, recalled for the assessment and then quietly left behind.
Education should enlarge the world available to students. Familiarity has a place, but it cannot set the boundary of what students encounter at school.
Schools should return to the model each year. Continual review does not mean replacing everything whenever an imperfection appears.
These questions will not make the curriculum decisions for a department. They do, however, establish what must come before a meaningful account of progression.
